history.content: Explain Article 14 briefly and cite it.
Article 14 ensures the State does not deny any person equality before the law or equal legal protection across India (Article 14, parent_0074).

source.text: 14. Equality before law.—The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.

history.content: Explain Article 15 briefly and cite it.

Article 15 bars the State and others from discriminating against citizens on religion, race, caste, sex or birthplace, forbidding any disability, liability, restriction or condition on those grounds (Art 15, parent_0074).
Restate the same answer in a single short sentence, preserving its citation.
Article 15 prohibits the State and others from discriminating against citizens on religion, race, caste, sex or birthplace (Art 15, parent_0074).

source.text:
15. Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.—(1) The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them.

(2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to—

history.content: Explain Article 16 briefly and cite it.

Article 16 guarantees equal opportunity in public employment, bars discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, etc., and permits reservations for backward classes, Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and residence criteria (Article 16, parent_0076).

source.text:
16. Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment.—(1) There shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State.

(2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office under the State.

(3) Nothing in this article shall prevent Parliament from making any law prescribing, in regard to a class or classes of employment or appointment to an office <sup>1</sup>[under the Government of, or any local or other authority within, a State or Union territory, any requirement as to residence within that State or Union territory] prior to such employment or appointment.

(4) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any provision for the reservation of appointments or posts in favour of any backward class of citizens which, in the opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in the services under the State.

<sup>2</sup>[(4A) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any provision for reservation <sup>3</sup>[in matters of promotion, with consequential seniority, to any class] or classes of posts in the services under the State in favour of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes which, in the opinion of the State, are not adequately represented in the services under the State.]

<sup>4</sup>[(4B) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from considering any unfilled vacancies of a year which are reserved for being filled up in that year in accordance with any provision for reservation made under clause (4) or clause (4A) as a separate class of vacancies to be filled up in any succeeding year or years and such class of vacancies shall not be considered together with the vacancies of the year in which they are being filled up for determining the ceiling of fifty per cent. reservation on total number of vacancies of that year.]

history.content: Explain Article 17 briefly and cite it.
Article 17 abolishes untouchability, bans all its practices, and makes enforcing any disability arising from it a punishable offence (Article 17, parent_0077).
Restate the same answer in a single short sentence, preserving its citation.
Article 17 abolishes untouchability, bars any resulting disability, and makes enforcement a punishable offence (Article 17, parent_0077).

source.text: 17. Abolition of Untouchability.—“Untouchability” is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of “Untouchability” shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.

history.content: Explain Article 18 briefly and cite it.

Article 18 bans non‑military/academic titles: India may not confer them, citizens may not accept foreign titles, and anyone holding a State office needs presidential consent to accept any foreign title, gift, emolument or office. (Article 18, parent_0077)

source.text:
18. Abolition of titles.—(1) No title, not being a military or academic distinction, shall be conferred by the State.

(2) No citizen of India shall accept any title from any foreign State.

(3) No person who is not a citizen of India shall, while he holds any office of profit or trust under the State, accept without the consent of the President any title from any foreign State.

(4) No person holding any office of profit or trust under the State shall, without the consent of the President, accept any present, emolument, or office of any kind from or under any foreign State.

history.content: Explain Article 19 briefly and cite it.

Article 19 assures every citizen the right to free speech, peaceful assembly, association, movement, residence and to practice any profession, subject to reasonable restrictions for public order, sovereignty, etc. (Article 19, parent_0078)
Restate the same answer in a single short sentence, preserving its citation.

Article 19 guarantees citizens’ rights to free speech, peaceful assembly, association, movement, residence and any profession, subject to reasonable restrictions for public order, sovereignty, security and morality (Article 19, parent_0078).
Explain Article 20 briefly and cite it.
Article 20 guarantees that only laws in force at the time can convict or punish, forbids double jeopardy, and protects against self‑incrimination. (Article 20, parent_0079)

source.text:
20. Protection in respect of conviction for offences.—(1) No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the Act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence.

(2) No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.

(3) No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.

history.content: Explain Article 21 briefly and cite it.
Article 21 guarantees protection of life and personal liberty; no one can be deprived of either except through lawful, established procedure. (Article 21, parent_0079)
Restate the same answer in a single short sentence, preserving its citation.
Article 21 ensures that no one can lose life or liberty except by a lawful, established procedure (Article 21, parent_0079).

source.text: 21. Protection of life and personal liberty.—No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.

history.content: Explain Article 21A briefly and cite it.
Article 21A mandates the State to provide free, compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen, as determined by law. (21A, parent_0079)

source.text: [21A. Right to education.—The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.]

history.content: Explain Article 22 briefly and cite it.
Article 22 ensures anyone arrested is promptly informed of the arrest grounds and entitled to consult a lawyer of their choice (22, parent_0079).
Restate the same answer in a single short sentence, preserving its citation.
Anyone arrested must be promptly told the grounds and may consult a lawyer of their choice (22, parent_0079).

source.text: 22. Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases.—(1) No person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest nor shall he be denied the right to consult, and to be defended by, a legal practitioner of his choice.

history.content: Explain Article 23 briefly and cite it.

Article 23 prohibits human trafficking, begar and forced labour, penalising violations; it permits compulsory public service provided there’s no discrimination by religion, race, caste or class (23, parent_0082).

source.text:
23. Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour.—(1) Traffic in human beings and begar and other similar forms of forced labour are prohibited and any contravention of this provision shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.

(2) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from imposing compulsory service for public purposes, and in imposing such service the State shall not make any discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class or any of them.

history.content: Explain Article 24 briefly and cite it.
Article 24 (parent_0082) bans hiring anyone under 14 in factories, mines, or any hazardous work, protecting children from dangerous employment.
Restate the same answer in a single short sentence, preserving its citation.
Article 24 (parent_0082) forbids employing anyone under 14 in factories, mines, or any hazardous work.

source.text: 24. Prohibition of employment of children in factories, etc.—No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment.

history.content: Explain Article 25 briefly and cite it.

Article 25 guarantees freedom of conscience and equal right to profess, practice, and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality, health; permits regulation of secular activities and opening Hindu institutions. (Article 25, parent_0083)

source.text:
25. Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion.—(1) Subject to public order, morality and health and to the other provisions of this Part, all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practice and propagate religion.

(2) Nothing in this article shall affect the operation of any existing law or prevent the State from making any law—

(a) regulating or restricting any economic, financial, political or other secular activity which may be associated with religious practice;

(b) providing for social welfare and reform or the throwing open of Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus.

Explanation I.—The wearing and carrying of kirpans shall be deemed to be included in the profession of the Sikh religion.

Explanation II.—In sub-clause (b) of clause (2), the reference to Hindus shall be construed as including a reference to persons professing the Sikh, Jaina or Buddhist religion, and the reference to Hindu religious institutions shall be construed accordingly.

history.content: Explain Article 26 briefly and cite it.

Article 26 says that, subject to public order, morality and health, each religious denomination may freely manage its affairs, including establishing and maintaining religious and charitable institutions (Article 26, parent_0083).
Restate the same answer in a single short sentence, preserving its citation.
Article 26 permits each religious denomination, subject to public order, morality and health, to manage its affairs and run religious and charitable institutions (Article 26, parent_0083).

source.text:
26. Freedom to manage religious affairs.—Subject to public order, morality and health, every religious denomination or any section thereof shall have the right—

(a) to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes;

history.content: Explain Article 27 briefly and cite it.
Article 27 says individuals cannot be forced to pay taxes whose proceeds are specifically used to support or maintain any particular religion or denomination (parent_0084).

source.text: 27. Freedom as to payment of taxes for promotion of any particular religion.—No person shall be compelled to pay any taxes, the proceeds of which are specifically appropriated in payment of expenses for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion or religious denomination.

history.content: Explain Article 28 briefly and cite it.

Article 28 bars state‑funded schools from providing religious instruction, except where the school is founded under a religious endowment, and forbids compulsory participation in instruction or worship without the individual’s or guardian’s consent (parent_0084, 28).
Restate the same answer in a single short sentence, preserving its citation.

Article 28 prohibits state‑funded schools from providing religious instruction and bans mandatory participation in any religious teaching or worship without the individual’s or guardian’s consent (parent_0084, 28).

source.text:
28. Freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or religious worship in certain educational institutions.—(1) No religious instruction shall be provided in any educational institution wholly maintained out of State funds.

(2) Nothing in clause (1) shall apply to an educational institution which is administered by the State but has been established under any endowment or trust which requires that religious instruction shall be imparted in such institution.

(3) No person attending any educational institution recognised by the State or receiving aid out of State funds shall be required to take part in any religious instruction that may be imparted in such institution or to attend any religious worship that may be conducted in such institution or in any premises attached thereto unless such person or, if such person is a minor, his guardian has given his consent thereto.

history.content: Explain Article 29 briefly and cite it.

Article 29 ensures minorities may preserve their distinct language, script or culture, and bars denial of admission to state‑funded schools on religion, race, caste, or language grounds. (parent_0085, Art 29)

source.text:
29. Protection of interests of minorities.—(1) Any section of the citizens residing in the territory of India or any part thereof having a distinct language, script or culture of its own shall have the right to conserve the same.

(2) No citizen shall be denied admission into any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving aid out of State funds on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them.

history.content: Explain Article 30 briefly and cite it.
Article 30 guarantees that religious or linguistic minorities may establish and run educational institutions of their choice (Art. 30, parent_0085).
Restate the same answer in a single short sentence, preserving its citation.
Article 30 gives religious or linguistic minorities the right to set up and manage their own schools (Art. 30, parent_0085).

source.text: 30. Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions.—(1) All minorities, whether based on religion or language, shall have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

history.content: Explain Article 32 briefly and cite it.

Article 32 guarantees the right to approach the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights and authorises it to issue writs (e.g., habeas corpus, mandamus) to protect those rights (parent_0089).

source.text:
32. Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by this Part.—(1) The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed.

(2) The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, whichever may be appropriate, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by this Part.

(3) Without prejudice to the powers conferred on the Supreme Court by clauses (1) and (2), Parliament may by law empower any other court to exercise within the local limits of its jurisdiction all or any of the powers exercisable by the Supreme Court under clause (2).

(4) The right guaranteed by this article shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided for by this Constitution.

history.content: Explain Article 39A briefly and cite it.
Article 39A requires the State to ensure the legal system promotes equal justice, providing free legal aid so no citizen is denied justice because of economic or other disabilities (parent_0092).
Restate the same answer in a single short sentence, preserving its citation.
Article 39A mandates the State to secure equal justice by providing free legal aid so economic or other disabilities don’t bar citizens from justice (parent_0092).

source.text: [39A. Equal justice and free legal aid.—The State shall secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice, on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall, in particular, provide free legal aid, by suitable legislation or schemes or in any other way, to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities.]

history.content: Explain Article 44 briefly and cite it.
Article 44 directs the State to work towards a uniform civil code for all citizens across India, ensuring common personal laws (44, parent_0093).

source.text: 44. Uniform civil code for the citizens.—The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.

history.content: Explain Article 51A briefly and cite it.

Article 51A lists citizens’ duties: respect Constitution, flag and anthem; uphold sovereignty; defend nation; promote harmony; preserve culture; protect environment; develop scientific temper; safeguard property; strive for excellence; provide education for children (6‑14). (parent_0094)
Restate the same answer in a single short sentence, preserving its citation.

Article 51A requires citizens to respect Constitution, flag and anthem; uphold sovereignty; defend nation, promote harmony; preserve culture, protect environment; develop scientific temper; safeguard property; strive for excellence; ensure education for children 6‑14 (parent_0094).
Explain Article 72 briefly and cite it.

Article 72 gives the President authority to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions and to suspend, remit or commute sentences, especially for offences tried by a Court Martial. (72, parent_0097)

source.text:
72. Power of President to grant pardons, etc., and to suspend, remit or commute sentences in certain cases.—(1) The President shall have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence—

(a) in all cases where the punishment or sentence is by a Court Martial;

history.content: Explain Article 110 briefly and cite it.

Article 110 (parent_0109) defines a Money Bill as one dealing only with (a) taxes, (b) government borrowing/guarantees, (c) custody of Consolidated/Contingency Funds, (d) appropriation, (e) charges, (f) receipts/audit, and (g) incidental matters; speaker’s certification final.
Restate the same answer in a single short sentence, preserving its citation.
Article 110 (parent_0109) defines a Money Bill as one confined to tax, borrowing, fund custody, appropriation, charges, receipts/audit, or incidental matters, with the Speaker’s certification final.
Explain Article 123 briefly and cite it.

President may issue urgent ordinances when Parliament is not in session; they act like Acts, must be presented to both Houses, lapse six weeks after reassembly or upon disapproval, and may be withdrawn anytime. (Art 123, parent_0115)

source.text:
123. Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament.—(1) If at any time, except when both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require.

(2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article shall have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, but every such Ordinance—

(a) shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament and shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament, or, if before the expiration of that period resolutions disapproving it are passed by both Houses, upon the passing of the second of those resolutions; and

(Part V.—The Union)

(b) may be withdrawn at any time by the President.

Explanation.—Where the Houses of Parliament are summoned to reassemble on different dates, the period of six weeks shall be reckoned from the later of those dates for the purposes of this clause.

(3) If and so far as an Ordinance under this article makes any provision which Parliament would not under this Constitution be competent to enact, it shall be void.
